questions.stemHtml: The initial segment, just between the peak of the axon hillock and the initial (unmyelinated) segment of the axon is also known as the trigger zone for the action potential. Initiation of nerve impulse occurs at the initial segment because?

options.label: A
options.text: It has a lower threshold than the rest of the axon

questions.answerText: It has a lower threshold than the rest of the axon
questions.solution: From a functional point of view, neurons generally have four important zones: multiple local potential changes generated by synaptic connections are integrated in a receptor or dendritic zone. a site where propagated action potentials are generated (the initial segment in spinal motor neurons, the initial node of Ranvier in cutaneous sensory neurons); an axonal process that transmits propagated impulses to the nerve endings; and action potentials cause the release of synaptic transmitters at the nerve endings In motor neurons, the initial segment is the portion portion of the cell with the lowest threshold for the production of an action potential (the portion of the axon at and just beyond the axon hillock) @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
From a functional point of view, neurons generally have four important zones:

  1. multiple local potential changes generated by synaptic connections are integrated in a receptor or dendritic zone.
  2. a site where propagated action potentials are generated (the initial segment in spinal motor neurons, the initial node of Ranvier in cutaneous sensory neurons);
  3. an axonal process that transmits propagated impulses to the nerve endings; and
  4. action potentials cause the release of synaptic transmitters at the nerve endings

In motor neurons, the initial segment is the portion portion of the cell with the lowest threshold for the production of an action potential (the portion of the axon at and just beyond the axon hillock)

questions.stemHtml: Electron transport chain has several complexes which throw the electrons from matrix to inter membrane space. The F1 portion of complex V has ATP synthase activity. What is the substance that blocks the transfer of ADP to ATP?
questions.solution: COMPLEX V - Has 2 Portions 1. F 0 Rolling gate Proton Ion channel present on IMM Attached to F1 2. F1 Protruding towards the mitochondrial matrix Has ATP Synthase activity Can convert ADP to ATP ADP to ATP conversion inhibited by → OLIGOMYCIN ADP to ATP transfer inhibited by → ATRACTYLOSIDE ADP – ATP TRANSLOCASE Present in IMM Has 2 surfaces - Bigger & smaller Transfer the substances by FLIP- FLOP MECHANISM Takes ADP IN ATRACTYLOSIDE - Inhibitor of ADP – ATP TRANSLOCASE OLIGOMYCIN Inhibitor of complex V Not an uncoupler It ligates F0 gate and closes it Inhibits both oxidation & Phosphorylation @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
COMPLEX V - Has 2 Portions

1. F0

  • Rolling gate
  • Proton Ion channel present on IMM
  • Attached to F1

2. F1

  • Protruding towards the mitochondrial matrix
  • Has ATP Synthase activity
  • Can convert ADP to ATP
  • ADP to ATP conversion inhibited by → OLIGOMYCIN
  • ADP to ATP transfer inhibited by → ATRACTYLOSIDE

ADP – ATP TRANSLOCASE

  • Present in IMM
  • Has 2 surfaces - Bigger & smaller
  • Transfer the substances by FLIP- FLOP MECHANISM
  • Takes ADP IN
  • ATRACTYLOSIDE - Inhibitor of ADP – ATP TRANSLOCASE

OLIGOMYCIN

  • Inhibitor of complex V
  • Not an uncoupler
  • It ligates F0 gate and closes it
  • Inhibits both oxidation & Phosphorylation

questions.stemHtml: A patient with right upper quadrant pain was diagnosed with gallstones and acute pancreatitis. Pancreas is supplied by various arteries. Arteria pancreatica magnum is one among them which is a branch of which vessel?
questions.solution: ARTERIA PANCREATICA MAGNUM Great artery to pancreas Br. of splenic artery Supplies pancreas Splenic artery Largest branch of celiac trunk Runs torturously on superior border of pancreas, gives multiple branches into pancreas, which forms anastomoses with substances of pancreas END ARTERIES TO SPLEEN No further anastomoses GASTRO DUODENAL ARTERY Passes behind the 1st part of duodenal Hepato pancreatic duct opens into 2nd part of the junction of fore gut & mid gut Proximal duodenal supplied by celiac trunk br. Distal duodenal supplied by br. of SMA Superior Pancreatico duodenal artery supplies head of pancreas & prox. Duodenum Sup. Pancreatico duodenal artery anastomose with Inf. Pancreatico duodenal artery (br. of SMA) on head of pancreas In posterior perforation of duodenal ulcer (less common than anterior) bleeding is form gastroduodenal artery In posterior perforation of gastric ulcer, splenic artery bleeds (present at bed of stomach) (less common) Rt. gastro epiploic artery supplies greater curvature of stomach @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ARTERIA PANCREATICA MAGNUM

  • Great artery to pancreas
  • Br. of splenic artery
  • Supplies pancreas

Splenic artery

  • Largest branch of celiac trunk
  • Runs torturously on superior border of pancreas, gives multiple branches into pancreas, which forms anastomoses with substances of pancreas

END ARTERIES TO SPLEEN

  • No further anastomoses

GASTRO DUODENAL ARTERY

  • Passes behind the 1st part of duodenal
  • Hepato pancreatic duct opens into 2nd part of the junction of fore gut & mid gut
  • Proximal duodenal supplied by celiac trunk br.
  • Distal duodenal supplied by br. of SMA
  • Superior Pancreatico duodenal artery supplies head of pancreas & prox. Duodenum
  • Sup. Pancreatico duodenal artery anastomose with Inf. Pancreatico duodenal artery (br. of SMA) on head of pancreas
  • In posterior perforation of duodenal ulcer (less common than anterior) bleeding is form gastroduodenal artery
  • In posterior perforation of gastric ulcer, splenic artery bleeds (present at bed of stomach) (less common)
  • Rt. gastro epiploic artery supplies greater curvature of stomach

questions.stem: The potential generated due to freely diffusible ion across a membrane is measured by which of the following equations?
questions.stemHtml: The potential generated due to freely diffusible ion across a membrane is measured by which of the following equations?
questions.solution: Nernst equation: A freely diffusible ion, having different concentrations on either side of a membrane, would diffuse through the membrane and reach equilibrium. Nernst equation, which describes the condition when an ion is in equilibrium across a membrane. Given values for [X]i and [X]o, X can be in equilibrium only when the voltage difference across the membrane equals the equilibrium potential (EX), also known as the Nernst potential. At equilibrium, the chemical and electrical potential energy differences across the membrane are equal but opposite. EMF (mV) = +/- 61/Z X log (C1/C2) C1 and C2: are the concentrations of the ion on either side of the membrane. Vm = Ex = -RT/ZxF ln (X)i/(X) R = the gas constant; T = temperature in degrees Kelvin; ln = natural logarithm; [X]i = the concentration of X inside the cell [X]o = the concentration of X outside the cell; Zx = the valence of charged molecules; F = the Faraday constant Vm = the membrane potential (Vm = Vi − Vo) Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz(GHK) equation is an expanded Nernst equation. It calculates the potential created by more than one ion, when these ions move from their higher to lower concentrations. Henderson Hasselbach equation: used to estimate the pH of a buffer solution Gibbs donnan equillibrium: In the presence of a non- diffusable ion, the diffusable ion distributes themselves so that at equilibrium their concentrations ratios are equal @Neet_pg_bot

A freely diffusible ion, having different concentrations on either side of a membrane, would diffuse through the membrane and reach equilibrium.

At equilibrium, the chemical and electrical potential energy differences across the membrane are equal but opposite.

EMF (mV) = +/- 61/Z X log (C1/C2)

C1 and C2: are the concentrations of the ion on either side of the membrane.

Vm = Ex = -RT/ZxF ln (X)i/(X)

R = the gas constant; T = temperature in degrees Kelvin; ln = natural logarithm; [X]i = the concentration of X inside the cell

[X]o = the concentration of X outside the cell; Zx = the valence of charged molecules;

F = the Faraday constant

Vm = the membrane potential (Vm = Vi − Vo)

Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz(GHK) equation is an expanded Nernst equation. It calculates the potential created by more than one ion, when these ions move from their higher to lower concentrations.

Henderson Hasselbach equation: used to estimate the pH of a buffer solution

Gibbs donnan equillibrium: In the presence of a non- diffusable ion, the diffusable ion distributes themselves so that at equilibrium their concentrations ratios are equal

questions.solution: The above clinical scenario is suggestive of Staphylococcal TSS [toxic shock syndrome]. Other Toxin mediated illnesses of Staphylococcus: 1. Food poisoning : Type A Enterotoxin is responsible for most of the cases of food poisoning. Incubatory Period: 1-6 hr due to preformed toxin. Site of action: The toxin stimulates the vagus nerve and vomiting center of the brain. It also stimulates intestinal peristaltic activity. Heat stable (not destroyed after heating food). Detected by ELISA, Latex agglutination test and toxin gene detection by PCR. 2. SSSS (Staphylococcal Skin Scalded Syndrome): due to exfolative toxins A & B. Scalded skin syndrome (Nikolsky’s sign-epidermal layer separated) Severe- Ritter disease (newborn), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) (adult). Milder- Pemphigus neonatorum, bullous impetigo. 3. TSS [toxic shock syndrome]: Multiorgan failure due to TSS toxin (enterotoxin F). Typically seen with history of usage of vaginal tampons. it is a super antigen non-MHC restricted activates > 20% lymphocytes without being processed by antigen processing cells (APC). leads to massive lymphokine release and shock. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The above clinical scenario is suggestive of Staphylococcal TSS [toxic shock syndrome].

Other Toxin mediated illnesses of Staphylococcus:

1. Food poisoning :

  • Type A Enterotoxin is responsible for most of the cases of food poisoning.
  • Incubatory Period: 1-6 hr due to preformed toxin.
  • Site of action: The toxin stimulates the vagus nerve and vomiting center of the brain.
  • It also stimulates intestinal peristaltic activity.
  • Heat stable (not destroyed after heating food).
  • Detected by ELISA, Latex agglutination test and toxin gene detection by PCR.

2. SSSS (Staphylococcal Skin Scalded Syndrome):

  • due to exfolative toxins A & B.
  • Scalded skin syndrome (Nikolsky’s sign-epidermal layer separated)
  • Severe- Ritter disease (newborn), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) (adult).
  • Milder- Pemphigus neonatorum, bullous impetigo.

3. TSS [toxic shock syndrome]: Multiorgan failure

  • due to TSS toxin (enterotoxin F).
  • Typically seen with history of usage of vaginal tampons.
  • it is a super antigen
  • non-MHC restricted
  • activates > 20% lymphocytes without being processed by antigen processing cells (APC).
  • leads to massive lymphokine release and shock.

questions.stemHtml: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in all of the following,except?
questions.solution: Types of necrosis 1. Coagulative It involves all the organs of body except CNS Most common reason: hypoxia There is formation of triangular structure called infarct: 3 “Tombsto0ne appearance” Example: zenker’s degeneration seen in patient suffering from enteric fever 2. Liquefactive necrosis Associated with abscess formation therefore associated with pyogenic infection it is seen in CNS A/K/a colliquative necrosis 3. Caseous necrosis “Cheese like appearance of Necrotic Material” Example: Tuberculosis, systemic fungal infection e.g. (Histoplasma, Coccidioidomycosis0 and in bacterial infections like syphilis. 4. Fibrinoid necrosis M: malignant hypertension due to damage to blood vessel as a result there is deposition of pinkish material in vessel wall A: Aschoff body (histological finding in rheumatic heart disease) P: Polyarteritis Nodosa Fibrinoid necrosis is associated with immune complex disease (Type III hypersensitivity reaction) ↓ Immune complexes damage the endothelial cells ↓ Associated with deposition of fibrin and fibrinoid material @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Types of necrosis

1. Coagulative

  • It involves all the organs of body except CNS
  • Most common reason: hypoxia
  • There is formation of triangular structure called infarct: 3 “Tombsto0ne appearance”
  • Example: zenker’s degeneration seen in patient suffering from enteric fever

2. Liquefactive necrosis

  • Associated with abscess formation therefore associated with pyogenic infection it is seen in CNS
  • A/K/a colliquative necrosis

3. Caseous necrosis

  • “Cheese like appearance of Necrotic Material”
  • Example: Tuberculosis, systemic fungal infection e.g. (Histoplasma, Coccidioidomycosis0 and in bacterial infections like syphilis.

4. Fibrinoid necrosis

  • M: malignant hypertension due to damage to blood vessel as a result there is deposition of pinkish material in vessel wall
  • A: Aschoff body (histological finding in rheumatic heart disease)
  • P: Polyarteritis Nodosa

Fibrinoid necrosis is associated with immune complex disease (Type III hypersensitivity reaction)

↓

Immune complexes damage the endothelial cells

↓

Associated with deposition of fibrin and fibrinoid material

Normal cases → Thoracic cavity @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Parts of intussusception Intussusceptum- incoming segment Intussuscepiens- receiving segment Neck- narrowest part of intussusception Apex - most prone to gangrene Middle layer is most prone to gangrene because it is sandwiched between outer and inner layer and has two acute bends Clinical features At time of attack ­ - Child cries a lot, pulls legs towards abdomen ­ - Colicky pain ­ - Bilious vomiting (Multiple episodes) In between attacks, patient is asymptomatic After many attacks ­ - Passage of small amount of stools mixed with blood (Red current jelly appearance) On examination Sausage shaped mass in right lumbar region Empty right iliac fossa known as Sign of dance Investigation Diagnostic + therapeutic - Enema (air > barium) Treatment Air enema (Enema creates pressure by which there will be reduction of bowel back to normal) For Recurrence - Air enema is repeated. If recurrence occurs for the third time - indication for surgery i.e. Ileocolectomy + Ileo- transverse anastomosis Radiological signs Plain x- ray Barium enema Ultrasound Meniscus sign Target sign Claw sign Coiled spring sign Target sign (transverse scan) Pseudo kidney sign (longitudinal scan) @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Parts of intussusception

  • Intussusceptum- incoming segment
  • Intussuscepiens- receiving segment
  • Neck- narrowest part of intussusception
  • Apex - most prone to gangrene
  • Middle layer is most prone to gangrene because it is sandwiched between outer and inner layer and has two acute bends

Clinical features

  • At time of attack ­

- Child cries a lot, pulls legs towards abdomen ­

- Colicky pain ­

- Bilious vomiting (Multiple episodes)

  • In between attacks, patient is asymptomatic
  • After many attacks ­

- Passage of small amount of stools mixed with blood (Red current jelly appearance)

On examination

  • Sausage shaped mass in right lumbar region
  • Empty right iliac fossa known as Sign of dance

Investigation

  • Diagnostic + therapeutic - Enema (air > barium) Treatment
  • Air enema (Enema creates pressure by which there will be reduction of bowel back to normal)
  • For Recurrence - Air enema is repeated.
  • If recurrence occurs for the third time - indication for surgery i.e. Ileocolectomy + Ileo- transverse anastomosis

Radiological signs

Plain x- ray Barium enema Ultrasound
  • Meniscus sign
  • Target sign
  • Claw sign
  • Coiled spring sign
  • Target sign (transverse scan)
  • Pseudo kidney sign (longitudinal scan)

questions.solution: Types of Parotidectomy 1. Superficial or lateral or classical parotidectomy For benign and malignant tumors involving superficiallobe Salivary tissue lateral to facial nerve is removed 2. Deep lobe parotidectomy For benign and malignant tumor involving deep lobe Salivary tissue deep to facial nerve is removed 3. Total conservative parotidectomy For benign and malignant tumor involving both superficial + deep lobe All salivary tissue is removed. Facial nerve is preserved 4. Radical parotidectomy For tumors invading facial nerve. All salivary tissue is removed + excision of facial nerve 5. Extended radical parotidectomy Radical parotidectomy + removal of adjacent structures (mandible, temporal bone, muscles) Surgical Landmarks for facial nerve S:Styloid process T: Tragal pointer, Tympanomastoid P: Posterior belly of digastric Ra: Retromandibular vein Complications of Parotidectomy Facial nerve paresis/paralysis Sensory abnormalities due to sacrifice of greater auricular nerve Frey's syndrome Parotid fistula @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Types of Parotidectomy

1. Superficial or lateral or classical parotidectomy

  • For benign and malignant tumors involving superficiallobe
  • Salivary tissue lateral to facial nerve is removed

2. Deep lobe parotidectomy

  • For benign and malignant tumor involving deep lobe
  • Salivary tissue deep to facial nerve is removed

3. Total conservative parotidectomy

  • For benign and malignant tumor involving both superficial + deep lobe
  • All salivary tissue is removed. Facial nerve is preserved

4. Radical parotidectomy

  • For tumors invading facial nerve. All salivary tissue is removed + excision of facial nerve

5. Extended radical parotidectomy

  • Radical parotidectomy + removal of adjacent structures (mandible, temporal bone, muscles) Surgical Landmarks for facial nerve
  • S:Styloid process
  • T: Tragal pointer, Tympanomastoid
  • P: Posterior belly of digastric
  • Ra: Retromandibular vein

Complications of Parotidectomy

Facial nerve paresis/paralysis

  • Sensory abnormalities due to sacrifice of greater auricular nerve
  • Frey's syndrome
  • Parotid fistula

questions.solution: The 5 H and 5 T of pulseless electrical activity → PEA implies that electrical activity is seen on ECG but the pulse is absent. questions.solution: Dissociative Amnesia: Commonest clinical type of dissociative disorder. Occurs mostly in late adolescence and young adults. Severe psychological trauma, the patient temporarily and unconsciously shuts down the memory of the traumatic event Circumscribed loss of traumatic memory is seen in these individuals The other memories are intact and this cannot be explained by normal forgetting Treatment: Supportive psychotherapy, cognitive therapy, hypnosis. questions.solutionHtml:
Dissociative Amnesia:

Commonest clinical type of dissociative disorder.

Occurs mostly in late adolescence and young adults.

Severe psychological trauma, the patient temporarily and unconsciously shuts down the memory of the traumatic event

Circumscribed loss of traumatic memory is seen in these individuals

The other memories are intact and this cannot be explained by normal forgetting

Treatment:

Supportive psychotherapy, cognitive therapy, hypnosis.

Identify trauma related cognitive distortions and help the individual cope with adaptive behaviours

Drug assisted interview could be beneficial to elicit information- abreaction (not recommended in children)

option b - it's not fugue, as all other memory functions would also be disturbed in fugue.

questions.stem: A 5 year old child presented with shock. Despite administration of High flow O2, normal saline and Antibiotics, the shock was not reversed. The Blood pressure was low and it was a cold shock. What is the next step of management?
questions.stemHtml: A 5 year old child presented with shock. Despite administration of High flow O2, normal saline and Antibiotics, the shock was not reversed. The Blood pressure was low and it was a cold shock. What is the next step of management?
questions.solution: CHILD WITH SHOCK 0 min – Start high flow O2 and establish IV/IO access. 5 min Push boluses of 20 ml/kg isotonic / NS upto 60 ml/kg, until perfusion improves or rales/ hepatomegaly appears. Correct hypocalcaemia and hypoglycaemia. Begin antibiotics If shock not reversed, It is Fluid refractory shock. 15 min Begin Ionotropes (Dopamine) Obtain central vascular access and airway if needed. If not improving, titrate Epinephrine (cold shock) or Nor epinephrine (warm shock). If shock not reversed, It is Catecholamine resistant shock. 60 min Begin Hydrocortisone Monitor CVP in PICU Maintain normal MAP – CVP & SCVO2 > 70 % Maintain Hb > 10 gm/dl If Shock not reversed, It is Persistent Catecholamine resistant shock. Rule out Pericardial effusion and Pneumothorax. If Shock not reversed, It is Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. @Neet_pg_bot

5 min

  • Correct hypocalcaemia and hypoglycaemia.

If shock not reversed, It is Fluid refractory shock.

15 min

  • Begin Ionotropes (Dopamine)
  • Obtain central vascular access and airway if needed.
  • If not improving, titrate Epinephrine (cold shock) or Nor epinephrine (warm shock).

If shock not reversed, It is Catecholamine resistant shock.

60 min

  • Begin Hydrocortisone
  • Monitor CVP in PICU
  • Maintain normal MAP – CVP & SCVO2 > 70 %
  • Maintain Hb > 10 gm/dl

  • If Shock not reversed, It is Persistent Catecholamine resistant shock.
  • Rule out Pericardial effusion and Pneumothorax.
  • If Shock not reversed, It is Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.

The patient underwent several ultrasound scanning to rule out whether she had appendicular mass or ovarian mass. Based on the ultrasound scan result, she was diagnosed with an appendicular mass. Whar would be the most appropriate management for this case?
questions.stemHtml: A 26 years old female was admitted to the hospital presented with abdominal pain for 1 week. The patient underwent several ultrasound scanning to rule out whether she had appendicular mass or ovarian mass. Based on the ultrasound scan result, she was diagnosed with an appendicular mass. Whar would be the most appropriate management for this case?
questions.solution: Management of Appendicular Mass If an appendix mass is present and the condition of the patient is satisfactory, the standard treatment is the conservative Ochsner-Sherren regimen. This strategy is based on the premise that the inflammatory process is already localized and that inadvertent surgery is difficult and may be dangerous. It may be impossible to find the appendix and, a fecal fistula may form. For these reasons, it is wise to observe a non-operative program but to be prepared to operate should clinical deterioration occur. CECT abdomen should be performed & antibiotic therapy (Metronidazole + 3rd generation cephalosporin or single dose of ertapenem) should be given. An abscess, if present, should be drained radiologically. Temperature & pulse rate should be recorded 4-hourly and a fluid balance record maintained. Clinical deterioration or evidence of peritonitis is an indication for early laparotomy. Clinical improvement is usually evident within 24-48 hours. Failure of the mass to resolve should raise suspicion of a carcinoma or Crohn’s disease. Using this regimen, approximately 90% of cases resolve without incident. The great majority of patients will not develop recurrence, and it is no longer considered advisable to remove the appendix after an interval of 6–8 weeks. Criteria for stopping conservative treatment of an appendix mass A rising pulse rate Increasing or spreading abdominal pain Increasing size of the mass @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A newborn baby presented with symptoms of jaundice, vomiting and failure to thrive. A diagnosis of Galactosemia was made using Direct enzyme assay. What is the toxic component that damages the Kidney and Brain in this condition?
questions.solution: GALACTOSEMIA Autosomal Recessive Deficiency of GALT (Galactose 1 PO4 Uridyl transferase) (MC), Galactokinase and Epimerase. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY Milk → Lactose → Glucose + Galactose Galactose can’t get digested in body due to Enzyme Deficiency Breast feeding is Contraindicated in Confirmed cases of Galactosemia GALT Deficiency → Accumulation of Galactose-1-Phosphate which is Toxic to Kidney, Brain and Liver Galactokinase Deficiency → Accumulation of Galactose and Galactitol which is Toxic to Eye CLINICAL FEATURES: Jaundice Hepatomegaly Seizures +/- MR Cataract ( Might be the only manifestation of Galactokinase Deficiency ) Diarrhoea / vomiting Failure to thrive Sepsis with E.coli is common in children with Galactosemia DUARTE VARIANT OF GALACTOSEMIA Quite Common Due to Single Amino Acid Substitution 50 % of Normal Enzyme Activity Present These Children usually remain Asymptomatic No Clinical significance of this Condition Diagnosis Reducing Substances in Urine Positive (detected by Benedict’s Test) Direct Enzyme assay Prenatal Diagnosis is also Possible TREATMENT Avoid Milk and Milk Products · Use Lactose free formulas @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
GALACTOSEMIA

  • Autosomal Recessive
  • Deficiency of GALT (Galactose 1 PO4 Uridyl transferase) (MC), Galactokinase and Epimerase.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

  • Milk → Lactose → Glucose + Galactose
  • Galactose can’t get digested in body due to Enzyme Deficiency
  • Breast feeding is Contraindicated in Confirmed cases of Galactosemia
  • GALT Deficiency → Accumulation of Galactose-1-Phosphate which is Toxic to Kidney, Brain and Liver
  • Galactokinase Deficiency → Accumulation of Galactose and Galactitol which is Toxic to Eye

CLINICAL FEATURES:

  • Jaundice
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Seizures +/- MR
  • Cataract ( Might be the only manifestation of Galactokinase Deficiency )
  • Diarrhoea / vomiting
  • Failure to thrive
  • Sepsis with E.coli is common in children with Galactosemia

DUARTE VARIANT OF GALACTOSEMIA

  • Quite Common
  • Due to Single Amino Acid Substitution
  • 50 % of Normal Enzyme Activity Present
  • These Children usually remain Asymptomatic
  • No Clinical significance of this Condition

Diagnosis

  • Reducing Substances in Urine Positive (detected by Benedict’s Test)
  • Direct Enzyme assay
  • Prenatal Diagnosis is also Possible

TREATMENT

  • Avoid Milk and Milk Products · Use Lactose free formulas

questions.solution: Drug of choice for hormone therapy in pre-menopausal patients - Tamoxifen Drug of choice for Hormone therapy in post-menopausal patients - Aromatase inhibitors Hormone therapy Estrogen has positive effect on breast cancer cells In hormone therapy either source of production of estrogen (ovary) is cut surgically or medically. Surgical method of stopping estrogen production – Bilateral oophorectomy Medical method of stopping estrogen production – Medical oophorectomy (block receptor of estrogen) In premenopausal females, ovary is the main site of estrogen production In postmenopausal females, estrogen is produced by peripheral aromatization from adipose tissues. (so, aromatase inhibitors are used in post-menopausal females). Treatment Ovarian ablation Bilateral oophorectomy LH/RH agonist (Goserelin, Leuprolide) SERM (Selective estrogen receptor modulator) - Tamoxifen - Raloxifene Aromatase Inhibitors (useful only in post-menopausal females) - Non-steroidal (Letrozole, Anastrozole) - Steroidal (Exemestane) Anti-estrogens - Fulvestrant Progestins - Megestrol - Medroxy progesterone acetate @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• Drug of choice for hormone therapy in pre-menopausal patients - Tamoxifen
  • Drug of choice for Hormone therapy in post-menopausal patients - Aromatase inhibitors

Hormone therapy

  • Estrogen has positive effect on breast cancer cells
  • In hormone therapy either source of production of estrogen (ovary) is cut surgically or medically.
  • Surgical method of stopping estrogen production – Bilateral oophorectomy
  • Medical method of stopping estrogen production – Medical oophorectomy (block receptor of estrogen)
  • In premenopausal females, ovary is the main site of estrogen production
  • In postmenopausal females, estrogen is produced by peripheral aromatization from adipose tissues. (so, aromatase inhibitors are used in post-menopausal females).

Treatment

questions.stemHtml: A 40 year old, right handed male presented to the ER with right upper arm pain. It was noted that he was a member of an amateur baseball team. Just prior to arrival he threw a ball and immediately felt a pop and sharp pain in his right upper arm. Following this trauma, which hormone is not released?
questions.solution: Metabolic and Neuroendocrine Response to Trauma or Surgery Injury Phase (Phase of catabolism) - Begins at the time of injury and lasts for 2-5 days - Phase of hypermetabolism - Stress hormones (cortisol, catecholamines, and glucagon) and volume control hormones (renin-angiotensin, aldosterone, and ADH) are increased. This leads to proteolysis, lipolysis, hyperglycemia and wound healing despite negative nitrogen balance. Turning Point: Transient period marked physiologically by turning off of the neuroendocrine response and clinically by the appearance of getting well. Early Anabolic Phase: Marked by a gain in muscular strength or positive nitrogen balance Late Anabolic Phase: Marked by a gain in weight and body fat or positive caloric balance @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Metabolic and Neuroendocrine Response to Trauma or Surgery

  • Injury Phase (Phase of catabolism)

- Begins at the time of injury and lasts for 2-5 days

- Phase of hypermetabolism

- Stress hormones (cortisol, catecholamines, and glucagon) and volume control hormones (renin-angiotensin, aldosterone, and ADH) are increased. This leads to proteolysis, lipolysis, hyperglycemia and wound healing despite negative nitrogen balance.

  • Turning Point: Transient period marked physiologically by turning off of the neuroendocrine response and clinically by the appearance of getting well.
  • Early Anabolic Phase: Marked by a gain in muscular strength or positive nitrogen balance
  • Late Anabolic Phase: Marked by a gain in weight and body fat or positive caloric balance

questions.stemHtml: A 45 year old female patient was rushed to the hospital after being involved in a house explosion with a resultant fire. A third degree circumferential burn in the arm and forearm region was noted. Which of the following is most important for monitoring?
questions.solution: Escharotomies When deep second and third-degree burn wounds encompass the circumference of an extremity, peripheral circulation to the the limb can be compromised. Development of generalized edema beneath a non-yielding eschar impedes venous outflow and affects arterial inflow to the distal beds. This can be recognized by numbness and tingling in the limb and increased pain in digits. Arterial flow can be assessed by determination of Doppler signals in the digital arteries and the palmar and plantar arches in affected extremities. Capillary refill can also be assessed. Extremities at risk are identified either on clinical examination or by measurement of tissue pressures >40 mm Hg. These extremities require escharotomies (release of the burn eschar by incising the lateral and medial aspects of the extremity). @Neet_pg_bot

  • This can be recognized by numbness and tingling in the limb and increased pain in digits.
  • Arterial flow can be assessed by determination of Doppler signals in the digital arteries and the palmar and plantar arches in affected extremities.
  • Capillary refill can also be assessed.

Renomegaly and progressive development of cyst occur. Development of bleeding in the cyst can occur and which can cause flank pain. High penetrance, variable expression (expressed in every generation but presentation will be variable) Clinical features: Usual age of presentation = 30 – 45 yrs 1. Flank pain (M/C) [Can be due to stone formation, bleeding in cyst → Gerota fascia stretch] Isolated Hematuria is not a feature of ADPKD. In contrast, gross hematuria will develop from rupture of the cyst, that communicates with the collecting system. 2. Stones incidence ↑ [M/C stone in polycystic kidney = Urate stones) (M/C kidney stone otherwise=Oxalate stones) 4. Rarely Can develop RCC: B/L multicentric (Severity is more) 5. GFR ↓ because cysts are progressively developing: Renin concentration­ ↓ Retention of Na → HTN, resulting in daily Headache & uremia if detected late. Extra renal manifestation (ADPKD): 1 Liver cyst (Lined by biliary endothelium) M/C extra renal manifestation Usually asymptomatic Pancreas cyst Spleen cyst 2. CNS a. Berry aneurysm → Subarachnoid hemorrhage, warning leaks → Excruciating headache. b. Arterial dolichoectasia → Malformation in the vascular supply of brain – predisposes patient to arterial dissection and can cause Stroke manifestation. c. Arachnoid cyst 3. CVS a. Mitral valve prolapse - Mid systolic clicks, late systolic murmur b. Mitral regurgitation c. Tricuspid regurgitation Pansystolic murmur 4. GIT → Colonic diverticulosis (Can present as constipation) (Lungs are usually spared in ADPKD) ADPKD → Has High Penetrance (Expressed in almost every generation) and Variable Expression. Clinical features:

  • Usual age of presentation = 30 – 45 yrs

1. Flank pain (M/C) [Can be due to stone formation, bleeding in cyst → Gerota fascia stretch]

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman presents at 17 weeks for antenatal evaluation as she had a history of delivering a baby with Downs syndrome. Which of the following is the next investigation of choice in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman presents at 17 weeks for antenatal evaluation as she had a history of delivering a baby with Downs syndrome. Which of the following is the next investigation of choice in this patient?
questions.solution: Because there is a past history of Down syndrome, a confirmatory test should be done. Amniocentesis and karyotyping are the best choice here. It is generally done around 16–18 weeks and gives confirmatory results. The triple marker is only a screening test and not a confirmatory test. USG can pick up soft tissue markers of Down syndrome, but it is not confirmatory, and USG can be normal in a fetus with Down syndrome. If the same patient presents at 11–12 weeks, then the answer is CVS and karyotyping. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Because there is a past history of Down syndrome, a confirmatory test should be done.

Amniocentesis and karyotyping are the best choice here. It is generally done around 16–18 weeks and gives confirmatory results.

The triple marker is only a screening test and not a confirmatory test.

USG can pick up soft tissue markers of Down syndrome, but it is not confirmatory, and USG can be normal in a fetus with Down syndrome.

If the same patient presents at 11–12 weeks, then the answer is CVS and karyotyping.

questions.stemHtml: A patient presented with a non insidious onset of mid abdominal pain. Examination revealed palpable abdominal mass. Past history revealed that the patient has a failed kidney. What is the investigation of choice for diagnosing this patient?
questions.solution: ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM (AAA) MC Site - Infrarenal aorta MC site of atherosclerosis - Infrarenal aorta MC causes of AAA - Atherosclerosis [ MC cause of Renal artery Aneurism – Medial Fibroplasia > Atherosclerosis ] MC symptom in AAA - Chronic vague abdominal pain / back pain (because location of aneurysm is retroperitoneal) MC & lethal complication of aneurysm - Rupture Most important predictor for rupture - Width / Diameter MC site of rupture - Left retroperitoneum Triad of AAA Sudden onset of midabdominal or flank pain Shock seen only in 1/3rd of cases Pulsatile abdominal mass Investigations X-ray - Eggshell pattern of calcification Investigation of choice for screening of abdominal aortic aneurysm - USG Investigation of choice for diagnosis & planning repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm - CT Investigation of choice for diagnosis & planning repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm in patients of renal failure - MRI Indications of surgery in AAA Diameter ≥ 5.5 cm / ≥ 5cm in females Symptomatic aneurysm Rate of expansion >1cm/year Atypical aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm, dissecting aneurysm, saccular aneurysm ) Management @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM (AAA)

  • MC Site - Infrarenal aorta
  • MC site of atherosclerosis - Infrarenal aorta
  • MC causes of AAA - Atherosclerosis [ MC cause of Renal artery Aneurism – Medial Fibroplasia > Atherosclerosis ]
  • MC symptom in AAA - Chronic vague abdominal pain / back pain (because location of aneurysm is retroperitoneal)
  • MC & lethal complication of aneurysm - Rupture
  • Most important predictor for rupture - Width / Diameter
  • MC site of rupture - Left retroperitoneum

Triad of AAA

  • Sudden onset of midabdominal or flank pain
  • Shock seen only in 1/3rd of cases
  • Pulsatile abdominal mass

Investigations

  • X-ray - Eggshell pattern of calcification
  • Investigation of choice for screening of abdominal aortic aneurysm - USG
  • Investigation of choice for diagnosis & planning repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm - CT
  • Investigation of choice for diagnosis & planning repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm in patients of renal failure - MRI

Indications of surgery in AAA

  1. Diameter ≥ 5.5 cm / ≥ 5cm in females
  2. Symptomatic aneurysm
  3. Rate of expansion >1cm/year
  4. Atypical aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm, dissecting aneurysm, saccular aneurysm )

Prostate needle biopsy by single core showed acinar adenocarcinoma predominant in cribriform pattern followed by crowded but separate glands and a minor component of 7% of single cell infiltrate not involving one half of a lobe. What is the stage of this tumor?
questions.solution: 8th AJCC TNM Classification for Ca Prostate Tis - Carcinoma in Situ Tla - up to 5% of tissue in resection for benign disease has cancer, DRE normal T1b - >5% of tissue in resection for benign disease has cancer, DRE normal Tic - Tumor is identified by needle biopsy T2a - Tumor involves one half of lobe T2b - Tumor involves more than one half of lobe T2c - Tumor involves both lobes T?? - Extra capsular extension on one or both sides including bladder Neck T3b - Seminal vesicle involvement T4 - Tumor is fixed/ invades adjacent structures other than seminal vesicle like External sphincter, Rectum, Levator muscles and or pelvic wall N0 - No regional Lymph node metastasis N1 - Metastasis to regional LN (obturator, internal iliac, External iliac, presacral) Μ0 - No metastasis M1a - Distant metastasis in non-regional LN M1b - Distant metastasis to bone M1c - Distant metastasis to other sites @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
8th AJCC TNM Classification for Ca Prostate

  • Tis - Carcinoma in Situ
  • Tla - up to 5% of tissue in resection for benign disease has cancer, DRE normal
  • T1b - >5% of tissue in resection for benign disease has cancer, DRE normal
  • Tic - Tumor is identified by needle biopsy
  • T2a - Tumor involves one half of lobe
  • T2b - Tumor involves more than one half of lobe
  • T2c - Tumor involves both lobes
  • T?? - Extra capsular extension on one or both sides including bladder Neck
  • T3b - Seminal vesicle involvement
  • T4 - Tumor is fixed/ invades adjacent structures other than seminal vesicle like External sphincter, Rectum, Levator muscles and or pelvic wall
  • N0 - No regional Lymph node metastasis
  • N1 - Metastasis to regional LN (obturator, internal iliac, External iliac, presacral)
  • Μ0 - No metastasis
  • M1a - Distant metastasis in non-regional LN
  • M1b - Distant metastasis to bone
  • M1c - Distant metastasis to other sites

questions.solution: Age <55 years any T, any N, M0 – stage 1 Any T, any N, M 1 – stage 2 Age ≥55 years Stage 1 - T1/T2, N0, M0 Stage 2 - T1/T2, N1, M0 and T3a/T3b, Any N, M0 Stage 3 - T4a, Any N, M0 Stage 4a - T4b, Any N, M0 Stage 4b - Any T, Any N, M1 Primary tumor (T) Tx = Primary tumor cannot be assessed T0 = No evidence of primary tumor T1 = Tumor ≤ 2cm in greatest dimension limited to the thyroid T1a = Tumor ≤ 1 cm in greatest dimension limited to the thyroid T1b = Tumor >1cm but ≤ 2 cm in greatest dimension limited to the thyroid T2 = Tumor >2cm but ≤ 4 cm in greatest dimension limited to the thyroid T3 = Tumor >4 cm limited to the thyroid, or gross extrathyroidal extension invading only strap muscles T3a = Tumor >4cm limited to the thyroid T3b = Gross extrathyroidal extension invading only strap muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid or omohyoid muscles) from a tumor of any size T4 = Includes gross extrathyroidal extension beyond the strap muscles T4a = Gross extrathyroidal extension invading subcutaneous soft tissues, larynx, trachea, esophagus, or recurrent laryngeal nerve from a tumor of any size T4b = Gross extrathyroidal extension invading prevertebral or encasing the artery or mediastinal Vessels from a tumor of any size Regional lymph nodes (N) NX = Regional lymph nodes cannot be assessed N0 = No evidence of locoregional lymph node metastasis N0a = One or more cytologically or histologically confirmed benign lymph nodes N0b = No radiologic or clinical evidence of locoregional lymph node metastasisN1= Metastasis to regional nodes N1a = Metastasis to level VI or VII (pretracheal, paratracheal, or prelaryngeal/ Delphian, or upper Mediastinal) lymph nodes. This can be unilateral or bilateral disease N1b = Metastasis to unilateral, bilateral, or contralateral lateral neck lymph (levels I, II, III, IV, or V) or retropharyngeal lymph nodes Distant Metastasis (M) M0 = No distant metastasis M1 = Distant metastasis @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Age <55 years

  • any T, any N, M0 – stage 1
  • Any T, any N, M 1 – stage 2

Age ≥55 years

  • Stage 1 - T1/T2, N0, M0
  • Stage 2 - T1/T2, N1, M0 and T3a/T3b, Any N, M0
  • Stage 3 - T4a, Any N, M0
  • Stage 4a - T4b, Any N, M0
  • Stage 4b - Any T, Any N, M1

Primary tumor (T)

Tx = Primary tumor cannot be assessed

T0 = No evidence of primary tumor

T1 = Tumor ≤ 2cm in greatest dimension limited to the thyroid

  • T1a = Tumor ≤ 1 cm in greatest dimension limited to the thyroid
  • T1b = Tumor >1cm but ≤ 2 cm in greatest dimension limited to the thyroid

T2 = Tumor >2cm but ≤ 4 cm in greatest dimension limited to the thyroid

T3 = Tumor >4 cm limited to the thyroid, or gross extrathyroidal extension invading only strap muscles

  • T3a = Tumor >4cm limited to the thyroid
  • T3b = Gross extrathyroidal extension invading only strap muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid or omohyoid muscles) from a tumor of any size

T4 = Includes gross extrathyroidal extension beyond the strap muscles

  • T4a = Gross extrathyroidal extension invading subcutaneous soft tissues, larynx, trachea, esophagus, or recurrent laryngeal nerve from a tumor of any size
  • T4b = Gross extrathyroidal extension invading prevertebral or encasing the artery or mediastinal Vessels from a tumor of any size

Regional lymph nodes (N)

NX = Regional lymph nodes cannot be assessed

N0 = No evidence of locoregional lymph node metastasis

  • N0a = One or more cytologically or histologically confirmed benign lymph nodes
  • N0b = No radiologic or clinical evidence of locoregional lymph node metastasisN1= Metastasis to regional nodes
  • N1a = Metastasis to level VI or VII (pretracheal, paratracheal, or prelaryngeal/ Delphian, or upper Mediastinal) lymph nodes. This can be unilateral or bilateral disease
  • N1b = Metastasis to unilateral, bilateral, or contralateral lateral neck lymph (levels I, II, III, IV, or V) or retropharyngeal lymph nodes

Distant Metastasis (M)

M0 = No distant metastasis

M1 = Distant metastasis

questions.solution: F508 mutation, Ch7, AR Abnormal CFTR protein This makes exocrine gland secretions CI- Rich. Thick and viscid So, clearance of secretions is decreased. Clinical features Meconium ileus (earliest manifestation) Delayed Passage of stool Pancreatic juice - Thick and viscid - (Stuck in pancreas and cannot liquefy meconium). IOC and TOC - Gastrografin Enema (enema will liquefy the stools) Recurrent Pneumonia Due to mucoviscidosis (stasis of lung secretions) ↓ Airways colonized by Pseudomonas and B. cepacia ↓ BIOFILM formation ↓ Bronchiectasis In western setup - early diagnosis and weekly Tobramycin nebulization to prevent primary colonization by these microorganism. Obstructive Jaundice (OJ) Bile is thick / viscid cholestasis→OJ Clay colored stools, dark yellow urine Secondary Biliary Long standing cholestasis → cirrhosis (May require liver Transplant). Endocrine pancreas also damaged - cell damage → Type 1 DM Failure to Thrive → Pancreatic juice stasis → Amylase ↓ in intestine → Sugar unabsorbed → Osmotic diarrhea (Reducing substance in stool). Infertility: causes Males - Agenesis of vas deferens Females - Cervical mucous plug. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• F508 mutation, Ch7, AR
  • Abnormal CFTR protein
  • This makes exocrine gland secretions CI- Rich.
  • Thick and viscid
  • So, clearance of secretions is decreased.

Clinical features

  • Meconium ileus (earliest manifestation)
  • Delayed Passage of stool
  • Pancreatic juice - Thick and viscid - (Stuck in pancreas and cannot liquefy meconium).
  • IOC and TOC - Gastrografin Enema (enema will liquefy the stools)
  • Recurrent Pneumonia
  • Due to mucoviscidosis (stasis of lung secretions)

↓

Airways colonized by Pseudomonas and B. cepacia

↓

BIOFILM formation

↓

Bronchiectasis

  • In western setup - early diagnosis and weekly

Tobramycin nebulization to prevent primary colonization by these microorganism.

  • Obstructive Jaundice (OJ)
  • Bile is thick / viscid cholestasis→OJ
  • Clay colored stools, dark yellow urine
  • Secondary Biliary Long standing cholestasis → cirrhosis (May require liver Transplant).
  • Endocrine pancreas also damaged - cell damage → Type 1 DM
  • Failure to Thrive → Pancreatic juice stasis → Amylase ↓ in intestine → Sugar unabsorbed → Osmotic diarrhea (Reducing substance in stool).
  • Infertility: causes
  • Males - Agenesis of vas deferens
  • Females - Cervical mucous plug.
